repo.description: Vim-fork focused on extensibility and usability
repo.name: neovim

body:
I return :bread:

## Problem

Healthcheck is blocking, preventing you from doing, well, anything, after `:che`.

related #35875


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7813eeb4-8416-4c2b-b06d-7a60e46f92ec

## Solution

Leverage the new vim.async api to make ONE existing healthcheck (namely, vim.health) non-blocking.

NOTE: **I have no idea if this is the right way to use the new vim.async API**. This PR more importantly serves as a way to disseminate knowledge and get more code using it in core than to fix #35875.

comment_data.body: One is sync and the other is async, the point of the PR. `await` yields to the event loop and is resumed when the `on_exit` callback in `vim.system` is called. `vim.system():wait()` blocks the main thread.

comment_data.body:
await() resumes caller context, which could be a fast event (AFAIK... don't want to just @ lewis on every single thing here). Here you can see resuming in a fast event:

```lua
vim.async.run(function()
  vim.async.await(3, vim.system, { 'true' }, {})
  local fast = vim.in_fast_event()
  vim.async.await(vim.schedule)
  print(fast, vim.in_fast_event()) -- prints "true false"
end)
```

comment_data.body:
Even for non-functions, I don’t see vim.b used much in Lua plugins. Module-local tables are preferred, despite needing manual tracking and cleanup.

Personally, I’m not sure we should try to push more usage towards vim.b. It was useful for Vimscript plugins, but having a shared namespace for each buffer makes it pretty undesirable for private plugin state.

I agree that lifetime management should be less ad hoc. My preference would be to look at how Lua plugins manage state now and build abstractions that support that. Being able to tie resources to a buffer's lifetime would be useful without requiring those resources to live in vim.b.

visibility is important, but it shouldn't be unconditional. This sort of stuff should be a developer choice. If someone really needs to dig down, then then`debug` module is always available which more or less has the ability to find any private state.

One disadvantage of visibility is that it prevents gc, unless your particularly careful and expose what you need via weak tables, but that is fairly advanced. And this is why visibility is a requirement on the event system since most handlers have no inferable lifetime (except for `once`).

comment_regular_data.body: Let's add this to the news once all healthchecks are updated.

> Healthcheck is blocking, preventing you from doing, well, anything, after `:che`.

What's there to do before `:chechealth` finishes? Running it is a deliberate decision with the intent to see the results. The only "other" thing to do here (to my eyes) is to be able to early stop if it runs too long or takes too much resources.

I am not particularly opposed to making this non-blocking if it adds relatively little complexity, but otherwise I wouldn't see this as an improvement.

What's there to do before `:chechealth` finishes?

I'd say the argument is that during a long (seconds) `:che`, it gives the impression that the editor is "stuck", which is bad UX. And while the checks are loading, it could be possible to execute other actions, e.g., switching to another tab to resume work.

> I'd say the argument is that during a long (seconds) `:che`, it gives the impression that the editor is "stuck", which is bad UX.

There is a progress update showing that there is some work... in progress.

> And while the checks are loading, it could be possible to execute other actions, e.g., switching to another tab to resume work.

I think needing to switch for several seconds of work is not a strong argument.

---

The benefit of adding async for `:checkhealth` would be if they can be executed in parallel. Not sure how feasible it is, since most of it is in-process Lua.

---

There is a similar use case of adding async where it does more disservice than good (in my experience): async `vim.lsp.hover()`. It is non-blocking and allows moving cursor before the floating window with hover information appears. Oftentimes it can take too long to appear which is too late after the cursor was already moved.

> There is a progress update showing that there is some work... in progress.

Yeah, but it does not render as a smooth experience at all.

> Oftentimes it can take too long to appear which is too late after the cursor was already moved.

If the cursor moves (or any other action that invalidate the operation) then an async hover should be cancelled. I'd imagine this is how it probably works in things like vscode.

> This PR more importantly serves as a way to disseminate knowledge and get more code using it in core

yes, this is an obvious use-case for vim.async and we should use it more. if it complicates things then that is a hint about how to improve `vim.async` ...
I believe this respects comments made in #41674. Justin, Lewis, mind taking another look? Thanks for the commentary.
